tools.name: search_guidelines
tools.description:
Look a rule up in the UMR guidelines (umr4nlp/umr-guidelines, guidelines.md).

keywords: terms to look for, e.g. "aspect", "modal strength", "have-rel-role-92", ":quant",
"reentrancy". Passages with more of the keywords come first, then those whose heading has
them, then those that mention them most.
max_results: how many passages to return (at most 10).

Returns {"sections": [{"heading": the passage's place in the guidelines ("Part 3. ... > Part
3-3-1. Aspect"), "text": the passage (a section, or a part of a long one)}], "found": how
many passages matched}.

tools.name: propbank_lookup
tools.description:
Look up a lemma and every alternate of it in PropBank (at most 20 per call).

language is "en" or "zh". Returns Markdown: per lemma, every roleset with its roles and all
its examples (the sentence, then each argument; traces such as *T*-1 are PropBank's own),
or "not in PropBank". Lemmas over the limit are not looked up: the last line names them
(call again with them). There is no PropBank for another language (Uzbek): nothing.

tools.name: search_annotations
tools.description:
Find how a case is annotated: gold UMR annotations of whole sentences.

language: "zh" (Chinese) or "en" (English).
keywords: words or pieces to look for, matched anywhere in a sentence or its annotation:
words of the text (e.g. "发生", "wanted to"), concepts ("have-org-role-91", "identity-91"),
roles (":ARG1-of", ":manner"), attribute values (":aspect state"). Sentences with more of the
keywords come first.
max_results: how many gold sentences to return (at most 10).

Returns {"gold": [{"doc", "sentence_number", "sentence", "annotation"}], where annotation is
the sentence's whole annotation (words, sentence-level graph, alignment, document-level
annotation); "found": how many gold sentences matched in all}.

Example 1: 联合国 安理会 ７月 底 作出 决定 ， 采取 “ 一切 必要 手段 ” 恢复 *OP* *T*-1 被 军人 推翻 *T*-1 的 海地 总统 阿里斯蒂德 的 权力 。

In order to annotate word senses, it is necessary to first have a sense inventory for all words that need to be sense-disambiguated. For languages that do not have a sense inventory, concepts can simply be represented by lemmas. For predicate concepts which the annotator wants to flag for later inclusion in a lexicon, the suffix -00 can be added to such lemmas. It is also possible that a language only has a sense inventory for a subset of the words. This is the case with English (1) and Chinese (2), where word senses are defined for predicates together with their arguments in *frame files*. 3-1-4 (1) The school has approximately 570 pupils. ``` (h/ have-91 :ARG1 (s/ school) :ARG2 (p/ pupil :quant (a/ approximately :op1 570)) :aspect State :modstr FullAff) ``` 3-1-4 (2) ``` 并且 还 有 很多 高层 的 人物 哦 ！ There will even be many VIPs! Scope for Quantification and negation To facilitate the translation of UMR into first-order expressions to support logical inference, we add a **scope** concept to represent the relative order of the predicate, quantified concept and negated concept. In most cases, the order of these elements are interpreted in textual order, and do not need an over scope annotation. The scope annotation is only needed when these elements are interpreted "out-of-order", as in (1). 3-1-5 (1) ``` Someone didn't answer all the questions (a/ answer-01 :ARG0 (p/ person) :ARG1 (q/ question :quant A :polarity -) :Pred-of (s/ scope :ARG0 p :ARG1 q)) ``` Related to scope is the issue of distributive vs. collective interpretations of events. Ambiguities in this realm may arise in a great number of different contexts. They may be triggered by, amongst others, explicit quantifiers or numerals, or events with plural arguments. For example, in (2) below, is there a single woman which every man loves, or does every man love a different woman?
